title: Measuring a proposed position clearly
description: A measurement is only useful when the reader knows what its endpoints represent.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A measurement is only useful when the reader knows what its endpoints represent. Start with the proposed position and the surrounding space rather than sending an isolated number.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Mark a reference corner or wall edge on a sketch. Record width, depth and height separately with units and the date. Label each measurement as approximate or checked. Add nearby openings and fixed obstructions so the available position is not confused with the desired object size.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A wall length of 240 centimetres does not mean a 240-centimetre piece is appropriate. The sketch should distinguish the wall, the proposed footprint and space whose use still needs discussion.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Does the number describe the room or the proposed piece?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Initial measurements are discussion inputs, not approved manufacturing dimensions. Do not assume photographs correct a missing measurement.

paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.

title: Recording a doorway and its opening direction
description: A doorway record needs more than a front-facing photograph.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A doorway record needs more than a front-facing photograph. The opening direction and what sits on either side can matter as much as the visible frame.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Photograph the doorway from both approaches. On a sketch, mark the hinge side, the usual open position and nearby obstacles. Record measured openings only where they can be checked safely. Note whether the door or fittings can change position; leave that as a question if unknown.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A wide-looking doorway may lead immediately into a narrow turn. Pairing the doorway view with the approach view prevents the opening from being considered in isolation.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What happens immediately before and after it?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: This is an access discussion aid. It does not certify that an object can pass through or authorize removing doors or fittings.

title: A first look at lift and staircase access
description: A first access survey should identify the points that need professional confirmation.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A first access survey should identify the points that need professional confirmation. It is more useful to record uncertainty than to conclude that a staircase or lift “looks large enough.”

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Sketch the sequence from arrival point to room. Identify lift entrances, internal lift space, landings and changes of direction. Record building restrictions you actually know and mark the rest as questions. Use photographs taken from safe positions; do not attempt to simulate carrying a heavy piece.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A lift may accommodate a footprint but still have a restrictive entrance or awkward approach. Recording these as separate locations helps the transport discussion.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Who can confirm the uncertain access details?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: No self-measured access sheet guarantees transport or installation. Serviceability, handling, charges and installation are confirmed individually under the current delivery policy.

title: Why a sketch needs units and a reference edge
description: A sketch without units can turn a helpful drawing into an ambiguous instruction.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A sketch without units can turn a helpful drawing into an ambiguous instruction. A named reference edge also makes later revisions easier to compare.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Put the unit in the drawing title and beside unusual measurements. Name one reference corner and measure from it consistently. Distinguish object dimensions from clear room dimensions. If a value is estimated, write that next to the value rather than relying on a general disclaimer elsewhere.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: Two arrows labelled 90 and 120 could mean centimetres, millimetres or an unfinished note. “Approximate centimetres, measured from window-side corner” gives the numbers an interpretable context.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A clean drawing is not automatically an accurate one. The person responsible for final dimensions must confirm the measurements before they become specifications.

title: Preparing photographs of a difficult turning point
description: A difficult turn needs a sequence of views.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A difficult turn needs a sequence of views. One close-up may show the obstruction while hiding how a piece would approach it.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Take an approach view, a view facing the turn and a view looking back, without entering an unsafe position. Number the photographs in travel order. Mark the same corner on an accompanying sketch and describe anything outside the frame, such as a railing or projecting fitting.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A corridor bend can look open in a photograph taken after the turn. Adding the approach view reveals why the turning point deserves closer assessment.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which restriction needs a measured check?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Photographs support a transport discussion but cannot establish turning clearance or a safe handling method. Do not attempt a risky trial movement.

title: Comparing a footprint with the space around it
description: The footprint of an object and the space used around it are different parts of a brief.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: The footprint of an object and the space used around it are different parts of a brief. Comparing both prevents a plan from considering only whether an outline fits.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Draw the proposed footprint separately from surrounding activities. Mark where chairs move, doors swing or people pause. Use paper shapes for a first comparison and label any dimensions approximate. Discuss the activity that creates the tightest condition rather than assuming an empty-room photograph represents daily life.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A table outline can fit between walls while chairs need additional space during use. The purpose of the sketch is to expose that question, not to prescribe a universal clearance.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: When is the position most crowded?
Which activity determines the next measurement?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Paper layouts cannot certify accessibility, safety or fit. Final dimensions and movement space need a specific review of the room and users.

title: Dimensions to discuss before a final specification
description: Dimensions become more meaningful when each is tied to a use or relationship.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Dimensions become more meaningful when each is tied to a use or relationship. A list of preferred sizes is a starting point for discussion, not a finished specification.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Separate overall dimensions, visible proportions and the room measurements supporting them. Record why each matters. Identify details that depend on another decision, such as a height related to existing seating. Leave unknown construction or mounting dimensions for the appropriate discussion.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A preferred console width may be about its relationship to a wall picture. Writing down that reason leaves room to revise the number while preserving the design intention.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Who will confirm the final specification?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Do not infer structural dimensions, load limits or mounting requirements from a visualization. Final design and dimensions require recorded approval.

title: Keeping approximate measurements distinct from approved dimensions
description: Approximate measurements are useful when their status stays visible.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Approximate measurements are useful when their status stays visible. Problems arise when an early estimate is copied into a later document without its qualification.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Add status, date and source columns to your measurement sheet. Keep the original estimate when a checked value arrives, but mark it superseded. Use one clearly labelled current sheet for discussion. If two sources disagree, record the disagreement and ask for confirmation rather than averaging them.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: An early sketch might say “about 180 cm.” A later checked value should not silently replace it in a screenshot that still appears to be the original drawing.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Is the current sheet easy to identify?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Neither repetition nor a polished layout turns an estimate into approval. Production dimensions remain a separate agreed record.

title: Documenting a change of room before a commission
description: Changing the intended room can change the brief even when the preferred object stays the same.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Changing the intended room can change the brief even when the preferred object stays the same. The new position deserves its own record rather than an informal note added to an old photograph.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Date the location change and identify the new room without unnecessary private detail. Review dimensions, access, light and surrounding objects again. List which preferences carry over and which assumptions no longer apply. Send the change against the existing inquiry reference when one exists.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A piece discussed for an open living area may later be considered for a hallway. The visual intention may survive while access and everyday movement questions change substantially.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What is different about the new position?
Which old measurements are no longer relevant?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A proposed relocation does not amend an agreed specification or confirm feasibility. Ask the atelier to review the change before treating it as accepted.

title: A measurement sheet an architect and client can share
description: A shared measurement sheet should make responsibility visible.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A shared measurement sheet should make responsibility visible. An architect, client and atelier may each contribute information without all confirming the same facts.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Give the sheet a title, date and version. Include a small plan, units, named reference points and a column for who supplied each value. Separate site measurements from desired object dimensions. Add unresolved questions and a place to record the later confirmation, rather than leaving a blank that could be mistaken for approval.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A client can identify a preferred position while an architect supplies a measured wall length. Keeping those contributions distinct makes the handover easier to review.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: The sheet does not allocate professional responsibility by itself. The parties still need to agree who verifies site conditions and final dimensions.
